--- title: "Tool 1 — Independent Fails" subtitle: "Why per-marginal sampling destroys the joint" --- *Learn-the-tool track · Lab 1 of 3.* This lab walks **one wrong move** — sampling each variable on its own — up the same ladder, from a toy whose answer you know by hand to the portfolio loss you stake capital on. The *idea* (resample each margin independently and watch the joint disappear) stays fixed while the **data grows more realistic at each rung**, and at the top the cost of the mistake is a single number: a Value-at-Risk (VaR — the size of a loss you only expect to be exceeded rarely) that comes out far too small. **What you will produce:** the **understated VaR** that an independent resample reports for a real bank book. Resampling each name on its own makes the banks look as if they diversify each other when they do not — the false sense of safety that the joint generators in the next labs exist to fix. --- ## 🧪 Rung 1 · Toy — Known Answer Start where the truth is not in doubt. `datasets.correlated_returns(rho=0.6)` draws a pair with a *known* linear correlation $\rho = 0.6$ — a single number for how strongly the two move together — so we can check by eye whether a resampling scheme keeps it. The point to take away: matching each variable's own histogram is **not** the same as matching the pair. ::: {#64608717 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} x_toy: Float[Array, "n"] y_toy: Float[Array, "n"] x_toy, y_toy = datasets.correlated_returns(n=2000, rho=0.6, seed=0) ρ_real: float = pearsonr(x_toy, y_toy)[0] # ρ = Cov(x,y)/(σₓ·σᵧ) the truth to preserve print(f"x, y: {x_toy.shape} built-in correlation ρ = 0.6 (the known answer)") print(f"measured ρ(x, y) = {ρ_real:+.3f} ← the truth to preserve") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` x, y: (2000,) built-in correlation ρ = 0.6 (the known answer) measured ρ(x, y) = +0.605 ← the truth to preserve ``` ::: ::: **The algorithm — resample each margin on its own.** An *independent resample* draws a new sample of $X$ and a new sample of $Y$ **with no regard for which $x$ went with which $y$**. The cheapest way to do exactly that is to **shuffle one column**: permuting $Y$'s rows leaves $Y$'s histogram untouched (it is the same numbers in a new order) but severs every original $(x, y)$ pairing. Spelled out, it is sampling the **product of the marginals** instead of the joint: ``` real ~ p(x, y) # the pairing kept independent ~ p(x) · p(y) # each margin alone — the pairing thrown away ``` ::: {#419d0a20 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} def resample_independent( x: Float[Array, "n"], y: Float[Array, "n"], seed: int = 1 ) -> Float[Array, "n 2"]: """Sample each margin on its own — draw p(x)·p(y), not p(x, y). Permuting a column keeps its histogram exactly (same values, new order) but destroys the row-pairing, so the result has the right *marginals* and the *independence* joint. This is the one operation the whole lab reuses. """ rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) return einx.rearrange( "n, n -> n (1 + 1)", rng.permutation(x), rng.permutation(y) ) # (n, 2): column 0 a reshuffle of x, column 1 an independent reshuffle of y indep: Float[Array, "n 2"] = resample_independent(x_toy, y_toy) ρ_indep: float = pearsonr(indep[:, 0], indep[:, 1])[0] # ρ after the row-pairing is severed print(f"marginals preserved? std y: {y_toy.std():.5f} → {indep[:, 1].std():.5f} (identical)") print(f"ρ(x, y) real = {ρ_real:+.3f}") print(f"ρ independent resample = {ρ_indep:+.3f} ← ρ destroyed") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` marginals preserved? std y: 0.01014 → 0.01014 (identical) ρ(x, y) real = +0.605 ρ independent resample = -0.011 ← ρ destroyed ``` ::: ::: The marginals are byte-for-byte the same; the correlation collapses from $0.6$ toward $0$. Read it as the whole lesson in miniature: a scheme can match every marginal perfectly and still throw the **joint** away. ::: {#cell-fig-toy-independent .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.6), sharex=True, sharey=True) for ax, (u, v), col, name in [ (axL, (x_toy, y_toy), COOL, f"real · ρ = {ρ_real:+.2f}"), (axR, (indep[:, 0], indep[:, 1]), CRASH, f"independent · ρ = {ρ_indep:+.2f}"), ]: ax.scatter(u, v, s=8, c=col, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none") ax.set_title(name, fontsize=11.5) ax.set_xlabel("x return") ax.set_ylabel("y return") ax.set_xticks([]) ax.set_yticks([]) despine(ax) fig.suptitle("Same marginals, different joint — the tilt is gone", fontsize=12) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The known-answer toy: real pair (left, ρ ≈ 0.6) vs the independent resample (right, ρ ≈ 0). Same two histograms on the margins — the resample only reshuffled the rows — but the tilted real cloud collapses into a round, structureless blob. Independent resampling keeps the marginals and erases the dependence.](lab-tool1-independent-fail_files/figure-html/fig-toy-independent-output-1.png){#fig-toy-independent width=1304 height=545} ::: ::: --- ## 🎭 Rung 2 · Toy-Real — A Stylized Market A round Gaussian blob never happens in markets. What *does* is the **joint crash**: two banks that drift together on calm days and plunge together on the bad ones. `datasets.two_banks()` is that stylized version — a shared driver plus a ~10% set of days where both names crater (the `crash_mask`). We run the **same** `resample_independent` on it and watch the co-crash — the lower-left quadrant where both names fall hard — empty out. What we are looking for is one number, `cocrash_fraction`: on the days one bank has one of its worst 10% returns, how often is the *other* bank also having one of its worst days? A high number means they tend to crash together; ~10% would mean they crash independently, as if by coincidence. ::: {#7fd1c243 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} a: Float[Array, "n_days"] b: Float[Array, "n_days"] crash: Float[Array, "n_days"] # boolean mask of co-crash days a, b, crash = datasets.two_banks(n=1500, seed=0) print(f"{int(crash.sum())} crash days of {crash.size} ({crash.mean():.0%})\n") indep_bank: Float[Array, "n_days 2"] = resample_independent(a, b) # the SAME op as Rung 1 cc_real: float = cocrash_fraction(a, b) # P(B crashes | A crashes) cc_indep: float = cocrash_fraction(indep_bank[:, 0], indep_bank[:, 1]) ρ_bank_real: float = pearsonr(a, b)[0] # ρ = Cov(a,b)/(σₐ·σᵦ) ρ_bank_indep: float = pearsonr(indep_bank[:, 0], indep_bank[:, 1])[0] print(f"co-crash real = {cc_real:.0%}") print(f"co-crash independent resample = {cc_indep:.0%} ← collapsed to the ~10% floor") print(f"ρ real {ρ_bank_real:+.2f} independent {ρ_bank_indep:+.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 160 crash days of 1500 (11%) co-crash real = 83% co-crash independent resample = 12% ← collapsed to the ~10% floor ρ real +0.89 independent -0.01 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-twobanks-independent .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.6), sharex=True, sharey=True) for ax, u, v, col, name in [ (axL, a, b, COOL, f"real · co-crash {cc_real:.0%}"), (axR, indep_bank[:, 0], indep_bank[:, 1], CRASH, f"independent · co-crash {cc_indep:.0%}"), ]: qˣ, qʸ = np.quantile(u, 0.10), np.quantile(v, 0.10) # the 10% crash lines box: Float[Array, "n_days"] = (u <= qˣ) & (v <= qʸ) # joint lower-tail quadrant: both ≤ Q₀.₁₀ ax.axvspan(u.min(), qˣ, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06) ax.axhspan(v.min(), qʸ, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06) ax.scatter(u[~box], v[~box], s=8, c=col, alpha=0.25, edgecolors="none") ax.scatter(u[box], v[box], s=22, c=CRASH, alpha=0.85, edgecolors="none") ax.set_title(name, fontsize=11.5) ax.set_xlabel("bank A return") ax.set_ylabel("bank B return") ax.set_xticks([]) ax.set_yticks([]) despine(ax) fig.suptitle("Independent resampling empties the co-crash corner", fontsize=12) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The stylized bank pair, real (left) vs independent resample (right), with the joint-crash quadrant shaded (both names in their worst 10%). Real crash days (red) pile into the lower-left corner — the co-crash. Resampling each margin on its own scatters those same red points at random, emptying the corner: the co-crash falls from ~83% to the ~10% independence floor while the margins are untouched.](lab-tool1-independent-fail_files/figure-html/fig-twobanks-independent-output-1.png){#fig-twobanks-independent width=1304 height=545} ::: ::: Same code, sterner stakes. The marginals still match, so each bank *alone* looks right — but the resample puts the co-crash at the independence floor. A risk model built on it would believe the two banks fall together only ~10% of the time, when in truth it is ~83%. That gap is what the next rung prices on real data. --- ## 📈 Rung 3 · Real — The Full Basket Now the real panel. We **reload** the prepared returns — there is no data cleaning to do here, because the steps from raw prices to daily log-returns already live in the data primer. We show a small corner of the table, then run the *same* `resample_independent` on a real pair of banks. The question is the same as the last rung: does the real co-crash survive when we shuffle the two names apart? ::: {#1e5e6397 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} R = datasets.load_returns() # prepared 14-name daily panel META = datasets.load_basket_meta() label = dict(zip(META["ticker"], META["label"])) print(f"{len(R)} trading days × {len(R.columns)} stocks " f"({R.index.min().date()} → {R.index.max().date()})") R[["JPM", "BAC", "XOM"]].iloc[:3].round(4) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4778 trading days × 14 stocks (2007-01-04 → 2025-12-30) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note icon=false} ## Where This Data Comes From The panel, its sectors, and the co-crash structure these names ride on are laid bare in the data primer — [Co-Movement & Co-Crashes](../../data/04-co-movement-and-co-crashes.qmd) builds the `cocrash_fraction` we read here. This lab reloads that panel and never re-derives it. ::: Take two real banks — JPM and BAC, the pair that falls together most reliably in the book — and resample them independently. The *only* new code is the reload; the operation is exactly Rung 1's: ::: {#5ceaed7b .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} jpm: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["JPM"].to_numpy() bac: Float[Array, "n_days"] = R["BAC"].to_numpy() indep_real: Float[Array, "n_days 2"] = resample_independent(jpm, bac) # SAME op — real series now cc_real = cocrash_fraction(jpm, bac) # P(BAC crashes | JPM crashes) cc_indep = cocrash_fraction(indep_real[:, 0], indep_real[:, 1]) ρ_jpm_bac: float = pearsonr(jpm, bac)[0] # ρ = Cov(JPM,BAC)/(σ·σ) ρ_jpm_bac_indep: float = pearsonr(indep_real[:, 0], indep_real[:, 1])[0] print(f"JPM · BAC real co-crash = {cc_real:.0%}") print(f" independent resample = {cc_indep:.0%} ← back to the ~10% floor") print(f" ρ real {ρ_jpm_bac:+.2f} independent {ρ_jpm_bac_indep:+.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` JPM · BAC real co-crash = 70% independent resample = 10% ← back to the ~10% floor ρ real +0.83 independent -0.01 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-real-independent .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.6), sharex=True, sharey=True) for ax, u, v, col, name in [ (axL, jpm, bac, COOL, f"real · co-crash {cc_real:.0%}"), (axR, indep_real[:, 0], indep_real[:, 1], CRASH, f"independent · co-crash {cc_indep:.0%}"), ]: qˣ, qʸ = np.quantile(u, 0.10), np.quantile(v, 0.10) # the 10% crash lines box: Float[Array, "n_days"] = (u <= qˣ) & (v <= qʸ) # joint lower-tail quadrant: both ≤ Q₀.₁₀ ax.axvspan(u.min(), qˣ, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06) ax.axhspan(v.min(), qʸ, color=CRASH, alpha=0.06) ax.scatter(u[~box], v[~box], s=6, c=col, alpha=0.18, edgecolors="none") ax.scatter(u[box], v[box], s=16, c=CRASH, alpha=0.7, edgecolors="none") ax.set_title(name, fontsize=11.5) ax.set_xlabel("JPM return") ax.set_ylabel("BAC return") ax.set_xlim(-0.15, 0.15) ax.set_ylim(-0.15, 0.15) ax.set_xticks([]) ax.set_yticks([]) despine(ax) fig.suptitle("Real co-movement, destroyed by per-marginal resampling", fontsize=12) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![JPM vs BAC, real (left) vs independent resample (right), joint-crash quadrant shaded. The real pair packs the lower-left corner — when JPM has a worst-10% day, BAC craters too on ~70% of them. Shuffling each column independently scatters those crash days apart, dropping the co-crash to the ~10% independence floor. The marginals — each bank's own return histogram — are untouched.](lab-tool1-independent-fail_files/figure-html/fig-real-independent-output-1.png){#fig-real-independent width=1304 height=545} ::: ::: The lesson survives the jump to real data unchanged: the independent resample keeps each bank's own tail (the marginals match) but throws away the fact that they fall **together**. On a single pair that is a vanished co-crash; on a *portfolio* it becomes money, which is the last rung. --- ## 💰 Rung 4 · Application — The VaR Understatement The deliverable is the cost of the mistake, in money. Reload the **portfolio loss target** from the [risk-measures primer](../../data/05-risk-measures.qmd): pick weights, form the portfolio return $r_p = \sum_a R_a w_a$ (each stock's return times its share of the book, added up), and define the loss as $-r_p$. **Value at Risk** at $1\%$ is then the 99th percentile of that loss — a loss this large or worse should show up only about 1 day in 100. We compute it two ways on a banks-only book: once from the **real** data, where the banks keep crashing together, and once from an **independent resample** of the same names, where that link is severed. What we are looking for is how far apart the two VaR numbers come out. ::: {#588fed26 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} BANKS = ["JPM", "BAC", "C", "WFC", "GS"] R_banks: Float[Array, "n_days d_banks"] = R[BANKS].to_numpy() w: Float[Array, "d_banks"] = np.full(len(BANKS), 1.0 / len(BANKS)) # equal-weight bank book def var_1pct(book: Float[Array, "n_days d"], weights: Float[Array, "d"]) -> float: """1% VaR of a portfolio loss. rₚ = Σₐ Rₐ·wₐ, loss = −rₚ, VaR₁% = Q₀.₉₉(loss).""" port: Float[Array, "n_days"] = einx.dot("day asset, asset -> day", book, weights) # rₚ = Σₐ Rₐ·wₐ return float(np.quantile(-port, 0.99)) # 99th-pct loss = 1-in-100-day level # Independent resample: shuffle EACH name's column on its own, severing the joint. rng = np.random.default_rng(7) R_indep: Float[Array, "n_days d_banks"] = np.column_stack( [rng.permutation(R_banks[:, a]) for a in range(len(BANKS))] ) var_true: float = var_1pct(R_banks, w) # real joint — co-crashes intact var_indep: float = var_1pct(R_indep, w) # independence — co-crashes erased understate: float = 100 * (var_true - var_indep) / var_true # % VaR shrinks under independence # Portfolio loss series for the figure: rₚ = Σₐ Rₐ·wₐ, loss = −rₚ port_true: Float[Array, "n_days"] = einx.dot("day asset, asset -> day", R_banks, w) port_indep: Float[Array, "n_days"] = einx.dot("day asset, asset -> day", R_indep, w) loss_true: Float[Array, "n_days"] = -port_true # loss = −return; right tail = bad days loss_indep: Float[Array, "n_days"] = -port_indep print(f"equal-weight bank book 1% daily VaR") print(f" real (joint) {var_true:.2%}") print(f" independent resample {var_indep:.2%} ← understated by {understate:.0f}%") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` equal-weight bank book 1% daily VaR real (joint) 6.72% independent resample 3.44% ← understated by 49% ``` ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-var-understatement .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, (axH, axB) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.2), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.6, 1]}) bins = np.linspace(-0.10, 0.16, 70) axH.hist(loss_true, bins=bins, color=CRASH, alpha=0.55, label="real (joint)") axH.hist(loss_indep, bins=bins, histtype="step", color=INK, lw=1.6, label="independent") axH.axvline(var_true, color=CRASH, lw=2) axH.axvline(var_indep, color=INK, lw=2, ls="--") axH.set_ylim(0, 320) # clip the calm-day peak axH.set_xlabel("bank-book loss (−return)") axH.set_ylabel("days") axH.set_title("Independent resampling thins the joint tail", fontsize=11.5) axH.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper right") despine(axH) axB.bar(["real\n(joint)", "independent\nresample"], [var_true * 100, var_indep * 100], color=[CRASH, INK]) axB.set_ylabel("1% daily VaR (%)") axB.set_title(f"VaR understated by {understate:.0f}%", fontsize=11.5) for i, v in enumerate([var_true, var_indep]): axB.text(i, v * 100 + 0.05, f"{v:.1%}", ha="center", fontsize=10, color=INK) despine(axB) fig.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The understated VaR. Left: the equal-weight bank-book loss distribution, real joint (filled) vs independent resample (outline) — same marginals, but the real tail reaches far further right because the five banks crash together. Right: the 1% VaR each implies. Resampling each name on its own thins the joint tail, so it reports a VaR roughly half as large — diversification the book does not actually have.](lab-tool1-independent-fail_files/figure-html/fig-var-understatement-output-1.png){#fig-var-understatement width=1305 height=489} ::: ::: Read the gap as capital. Each bank's own loss histogram is matched exactly, so a naive check on the marginals would sign off — yet the independent resample reports a $1\%$ VaR roughly **half** what the real joint demands. The error is not in any one name; it is in the *joint*: shuffling each column away from the others manufactures a diversification the bank book does not have, precisely on the systemic days when the banks fall as one. That is the entire case for joint sampling. Getting each bank's own histogram right is necessary but never enough; the tail risk lives in how the names move together, and only a generator that draws from the joint $p(x, y)$ — not the product $p(x)\,p(y)$ — can carry it. And keeping the correlation is not enough either: if you keep $\rho$ but still assume the crashes are milder than they really are, the VaR is wrong again, just less obviously. That is the failure [Tool 2 · Gaussian Monte-Carlo](lab-tool2-gaussian-mc.qmd) takes up next.
